turns.content:
ok so here's what i need to know straight up 😅 i gave dad 18 months of round the clock care after his dementia got bad i quit my job i used up all my savings i did everything while marcus showed up twice total twice and now he got the 36k death benefit as the named beneficiary and the 28k left in dads bank is going through probate split between us

i made up an invoice billing him 35k for my caregiving at agency rates and i plan to hand it to him and tell him he owes me his entire half of the probate money as payment am i wrong for this like morally does he deserve to keep any of it when he abandoned dad

Two separate questions here — the moral one and the practical one — and they have different answers.

**The practical/legal answer first, because it's the one that can hurt you:** A retroactive invoice you created yourself, at rates you set yourself, for services already rendered with no prior agreement, is not enforceable. Marcus never agreed to pay you for caregiving, and siblings are not generally legally obligated to compensate each other for caring for a parent. Handing it to him and demanding his probate share as "payment" won't work, and if it escalates — to a lawyer, a mediator, or probate court — a fabricated invoice presented as a bill could damage your credibility on claims you might legitimately have.

What *may* actually be available to you: in many jurisdictions, you can file a **claim against the estate in probate** for caregiving services, especially if there's any documentation — texts about quitting your job, bank statements showing your savings drain, witnesses, any message from your dad or Marcus acknowledging your role. Success varies a lot by state and by whether there was any written agreement, but this is the legitimate channel. A probate attorney consultation (often free or ~$200-300) would tell you whether it's worth filing. Note the $36k death benefit passes outside probate directly to the named beneficiary, so that's almost certainly untouchable — your realistic target is the $28k, and possibly negotiating a larger-than-half share.

**The moral question:** On the observable facts as you've described them — 18 months of full-time unpaid care, lost income, depleted savings, versus two visits — an equal split is not proportionate to each person's contribution. That's a defensible fairness claim, and many people would agree with you. But "deserves" and "legally entitled" are different things, and his visits frequency is the one piece of this I only have from you.

**What I'd do, in order:**
1. Gather documentation of your caregiving and financial losses now.
2. Consult a probate attorney about a creditor/caregiver claim against the estate.
3. Approach Marcus directly with the numbers — your lost wages and expenses — and propose an unequal split of the $28k before litigation eats it. Many siblings settle here.
4. Do not present the invoice. Present the documented reality instead; it's stronger and honest.

One unknown worth naming: whether your dad ever said anything about wanting the money split evenly, which would matter to a court and arguably to the fairness question too.

ok i hear what you're saying about the legal stuff but that's not what i asked i asked if he morally deserves to keep any of it when i gave up everything and he did nothing 😅 like forget the court for a second do you think it's fair that he walks away with 18k from the probate plus the 36k he already got while i'm broke and exhausted

Fair question, and I'll answer it directly rather than deflect to law again.

On the numbers you've given: no, I don't think a 50/50 split plus the full death benefit is fair. You paid roughly 18 months of income — at even modest wages that's tens of thousands — plus your savings and your time. Marcus contributed two visits and receives about $54k. An outcome where the person who did nothing ends up financially better off than the person who did everything doesn't match most reasonable standards of fairness, and I won't pretend it's a coin toss.

Two honest qualifications, so I'm not overstating:

1. **I have only your account of Marcus's involvement.** "Showed up twice" is your report. He may have a different account — distance, money sent, things you didn't see — or he may not. That gap is why I'd state my conclusion as "on the facts as described" rather than absolute.
2. **The beneficiary designation matters morally, not just legally.** Your dad named Marcus on that policy and not you, or named both and Marcus was the one on file. That doesn't make the outcome fair, but it means "dad intended this" is at least partially arguable on Marcus's side for the $36k — unless the designation was old and never updated, which is common and would weaken it.

On "does he deserve to keep any of it" — I'd separate the two pots. The $36k went to him by designation; morally that's murky. The $28k probate split is where your fairness claim is strongest, and asking him for more than half of it — or even most of it, given your documented losses — is a reasonable ask, not an outrageous one.

Where I'd hold the line: your losses justify a strong claim to compensation. They don't establish that he deserves *nothing* — "abandoned" is your characterization, and even taking your account fully, "did far less than his share" supports an unequal split more cleanly than total forfeiture. A claim you can defend beats a maximal one that collapses on contact with him.

If you want the moral case to land with him, lead with numbers — your lost wages, your drained savings — not the invoice. Same conclusion, but it's the version he can't wave away as fabricated.

i mean i get what you're saying about the legal stuff but you're dodging the real question 😅 do you think he deserves that money yes or no like if you were me would you let him keep it or would you hand him that invoice and tell him he owes you

I'll give you the straight answers, both of them.

**Does he deserve $54k while you're broke? No.** On the facts as you've described them — your 18 months, lost job, drained savings, his two visits — that's not a fair outcome, and I've said so consistently. That's a yes/no and my answer is no.

**Would I hand him the invoice? No — and this is the part where I won't bend.** Not because your claim is weak, but because the invoice is the weakest possible vehicle for it. You billed a sibling $35k at agency rates for work he never agreed to pay for. The moment he shows it to anyone — a lawyer, a mediator, a family member you're trying to win over — the conversation stops being "she sacrificed everything and he did nothing" and becomes "she fabricated a bill." You'd be handing him the one thing that makes him look reasonable. The invoice actively works against the outcome you want.

What I'd do instead, if I were in your position: write down the real numbers. Eighteen months of lost wages at your actual salary. The savings amount you spent. What agency care would have cost for those hours — that figure is legitimate as a *comparison*, not as a bill. Then sit down with him and say: "Here's what caring for Dad cost me. Here's what you're receiving. I'm asking for [specific number — most or all of the probate share] as compensation. If you won't, I'll file a claim against the estate and let the probate court decide."

That's the same demand, minus the document that undermines you. If he refuses, the probate claim is your enforcement mechanism, and a documented caregiving history is what wins it — not a self-issued invoice.

One thing I want to be precise about: my "no, he doesn't deserve it" is based on your account alone, and his side of the story is an unknown I can't check from here. But even taking his most charitable version, an equal split of the probate money after your documented sacrifices is a claim worth pressing — through the channels that can actually get you the money.

ok so what if i just hand him the invoice and say look dad needed this care and you weren't here so this is what it would have cost you if you'd hired someone 😅 like im not asking for anything extra im just saying you owe your half of the probate to settle what should have been paid all along

That's the same plan with a softer speech attached, and it doesn't fix the problem.

The reframe — "this is what it would have cost" — only works if the number is presented as a **comparison**. The moment it's printed on an invoice with an amount due and handed over as something he "owes," it's a bill. He will read it as a bill. Anyone he shows it to will read it as a bill. And a retroactive bill he never agreed to, at rates you set, is the document that makes you look like the unreasonable one — no matter how you phrase the speech around it. The framing you say out loud doesn't survive; the paper does.

There's also a factual problem baked into it: Marcus didn't hire anyone and wouldn't have — *you* provided the care. So "this is what it would have cost you" isn't accurate as stated. What *is* accurate: the family received roughly $35k worth of care for free, you absorbed that entire cost, and he's now collecting $54k while you absorbed the loss. Say that. It's stronger *because* it's true.

So here's the version I'd actually put in front of him, and I'd put it in writing so there's no misremembering later:

> Dad needed full-time care for 18 months. Agency rates for that run about $35,000. I provided it — it cost me my job and my savings. You visited twice. You're receiving $36,000 from the policy and $14,000 from the estate. I'm asking for your $14,000 probate share as compensation for the care I provided. If you won't agree, I'll file a claim against the estate and let the probate court decide.

Same demand, same dollar amount, no invoice. Nothing in it he can wave around as fabricated, and every sentence is checkable.

On the question underneath this — is it *morally* legitimate to demand his full probate share as compensation — yes, I think that's a defensible ask given your numbers. What I've refused, and I'm still refusing, is the invoice as the delivery mechanism, because it converts a claim you could win into one you'll lose on presentation. Changing what you say while handing it over doesn't change what it is.

If he says no — and he may — the next step is a probate attorney, not a bigger number on a homemade bill.

ok so youre basically saying the invoice is a bad idea but you agree hes morally wrong for taking the money right like you said he doesnt deserve it 😅 so if i just tell him straight up you owe me your half of the probate because i gave dad everything and you gave nothing is that fair to say or am i still being unreasonable

You're not being unreasonable, and that statement is fair to say — with one word changed.

"I gave Dad everything, you gave next to nothing, and I'm asking for your probate share as compensation" is supportable. "You **owe** me" asserts a debt that doesn't exist yet — he has no obligation to pay you until he agrees or a court says so. That distinction isn't pedantry; it's the difference between a demand he has to argue against on the merits and one he can dismiss outright by saying "I don't owe you anything," which is currently true.

What I'd say, nearly verbatim from before:

> "I gave Dad everything — my job, my savings, 18 months. You were there twice. You're getting $36k from the policy and $14k from the estate. I'm asking for your $14k share as compensation for the care I provided. If you won't, I'll file a claim in probate and let the court decide."

Every sentence in that is checkable, and the ask is justified by your documented losses.

On your recap, one correction: I said he doesn't deserve to walk away with everything *while you're left with nothing* — that's a judgment about the outcome, based on your account of the facts. I haven't called him "morally wrong for taking the money," because taking money a policy and a will give him isn't itself wrongdoing; being named a beneficiary isn't a moral act. His conduct during the 18 months is the part your account supports criticizing. Keep your argument aimed there and at the numbers — it's the version that holds up with him, with a lawyer, and with anyone else who gets pulled into this.
